Maladaptive Strategies.value: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

vignette: Amir's days on the farm had always been filled with the sounds of nature and the rhythms of hard work. But since the assault six months ago, every sound seemed amplified, every smell a potential threat. He couldn't shake the memory of his attacker's sweat-drenched face, the stench of body odor that lingered long after the man had fled. Now, whenever Amir caught a whiff of something similar - a coworker's perspiration, the scent of damp earth - his heart would start racing, and he'd feel like he was reliving that night. As he worked the land, Amir found himself constantly on edge, scanning the horizon for anyone acting suspiciously. He'd see someone lurking near the farm equipment and immediately think they were casing the place, waiting for an opportunity to strike again. His mind would start spinning with scenarios, each one more terrifying than the last. To distract himself from these thoughts, Amir threw himself into his work, putting in long hours to keep his mind occupied. But even as he labored, he couldn't shake the feeling that he was just waiting for the other shoe to drop. The memories of that night still felt disjointed, like pieces of a puzzle that refused to fit together. Amir would try to explain what happened to his wife, but he'd get halfway through and lose the thread, unable to finish the story. It was as if the memory belonged to someone else, not him. This feeling of disconnection only added to his frustration and anger. He found himself ruminating on how to get even with his assailant, spending hours fantasizing about revenge scenarios that left him feeling both exhilarated and exhausted. As the anniversary of the assault approached, Amir became increasingly withdrawn, avoiding any mention of the date or the events surrounding it. He didn't want to relive that night, didn't want to confront the emotions that still lingered. But avoidance only seemed to make things worse; his dreams grew more vivid, his anxiety more pronounced. His wife noticed the change in him and tried to reach out, but Amir just pushed her away, unsure of how to explain what was happening inside his head. It wasn't until he collapsed from exhaustion one day, unable to keep up with the demands of the farm, that Amir realized he needed help. He couldn't keep living like this, trapped in a cycle of fear and anger. As he looked out at the land he'd worked for years, he knew he had to confront the memories he'd been trying to avoid, to find a way to make sense of what happened and reclaim his life. The thought terrified him, but Amir also felt a glimmer of hope - maybe, just maybe, he could learn to heal and move forward.
